\boxed{f(n)=n-3,\qquad g(n)=\left\lfloor\frac{2n}{3}\right\rfloor-1}

**Non-adaptive.** Querying $n-3$ people leaves three unqueried. The answers determine every edge incident to a queried person, hence for each unqueried person we know how many of his neighbours are also unqueried. With three vertices this fixes the (at most one) edge among them, so the whole undirected cycle is determined. If only $n-4$ queries are made, an adversary places the four unqueried people consecutively as $a,b,c,d$ and uses either $a\!-\!b\!-\!c\!-\!d$ or $a\!-\!c\!-\!b\!-\!d$; every queried person has the same two neighbours in both cases, yet the two seatings are not reversals of each other. Thus $f(n)=n-3$.

**Adaptive.** Query anyone first; this reveals a path of $k=n-3$ unknown people between two known endpoints. Let $p(k)$ be the optimal worst-case number of further queries for such a path. Querying an unknown person either fixes two consecutive positions (if he lies next to an endpoint) or fixes three consecutive positions but creates an orientation ambiguity costing one extra query. This gives $p(0)=p(1)=0,\;p(2)=1$ and
$$p(k)=1+\max\Bigl\{p(k-2),\;1+\min_{0\le i\le k-2}\bigl(p(i)+p(k-2-i)\bigr)\Bigr\},$$
whose solution is $p(k)=\lfloor 2k/3\rfloor$. An adversary can always force this bound, so it is tight. Hence
$$g(n)=1+p(n-3)=1+\Bigl\lfloor\frac{2(n-3)}{3}\Bigr\rfloor=\Bigl\lfloor\frac{2n}{3}\Bigr\rfloor-1.$$

\boxed{f(n)=n-3,\qquad g(n)=\left\lfloor\frac{2n}{3}\right\rfloor-1}

**Non-adaptive.** Querying $n-3$ people leaves three unqueried. The answers determine every edge incident to a queried person, hence for each unqueried person we know how many of his neighbours are also unqueried. With three vertices this fixes the (at most one) edge among them, so the whole undirected cycle is determined. If only $n-4$ queries are made, an adversary places the four unqueried people consecutively as $a,b,c,d$ and uses either $a\!-\!b\!-\!c\!-\!d$ or $a\!-\!c\!-\!b\!-\!d$; every queried person has the same two neighbours in both cases, yet the two seatings are not reversals of each other. Thus $f(n)=n-3$.

**Adaptive.** Query anyone first; this reveals a path of $k=n-3$ unknown people between two known endpoints. Let $p(k)$ be the optimal worst-case number of further queries for such a path. Querying an unknown person either fixes two consecutive positions (if he lies next to an endpoint) or fixes three consecutive positions but creates an orientation ambiguity costing one extra query. This gives $p(0)=p(1)=0,\;p(2)=1$ and
$$p(k)=1+\max\Bigl\{p(k-2),\;1+\min_{0\le i\le k-2}\bigl(p(i)+p(k-2-i)\bigr)\Bigr\},$$
whose solution is $p(k)=\lfloor 2k/3\rfloor$. An adversary can always force this bound, so it is tight. Hence
$$g(n)=1+p(n-3)=1+\Bigl\lfloor\frac{2(n-3)}{3}\Bigr\rfloor=\Bigl\lfloor\frac{2n}{3}\Bigr\rfloor-1.$$
